entities.name: Cináed mac Írgalaig
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cináed mac Írgalaig (born 601 CE, died 728 CE), known also as Cináed Cáech, "the one-eyed," was a pivotal figure in early medieval Irish history, reigning as King of Brega and briefly holding the High Kingship of Ireland from 724 to 728 CE. A member of the Uí Chonaing branch of the Síl nÁedo Sláine, a dominant sub-sept of the Southern Uí Néill, Cináed emerged during a period of intense dynastic competition. His ascent marked a significant, albeit temporary, challenge to the traditional succession patterns among the Uí Néill, demonstrating the fluid nature of power and the ever-present threat of internal conflict within the powerful Irish royal lineages.

Cináed's rise to prominence was cemented by his military victories. In 718 CE, he triumphed at the Battle of Cenannus, a crucial engagement that solidified the Uí Chonaing's control over Brega, the fertile plains north of Dublin. His most celebrated achievement, however, came at the Battle of Almain (modern Allen, County Kildare) in 722 CE. Here, Cináed decisively defeated Fergal mac Máele Dúin, then High King of Ireland and a formidable rival from the Cenél nÉogain branch of the Northern Uí Néill. This victory, described in annals as a catastrophic defeat for Fergal's forces, directly led to Cináed's assumption of the High Kingship in 724 CE, breaking a long-standing pattern of succession and briefly asserting the dominance of the Síl nÁedo Sláine.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cináed mac Írgalaig's decisive victory at the Battle of Almain and his subsequent four-year reign as High King profoundly impacted the dynastic succession of the Uí Néill, temporarily disrupting Northern Uí Néill hegemony and cementing the regional power of the Uí Chonaing.
